content.p: On the evening of Friday 13 November 2015, three teams of gunmen and suicide bombers struck the Paris region within about half an hour of one another. They hit the area around the Stade de France, where France was playing Germany in a friendly football match, then bars and restaurants in the 10th and 11th arrondissements, and finally the Bataclan concert hall, where the American band Eagles of Death Metal was playing to a sold-out crowd. The Islamic State group claimed responsibility the next day.

The attacks killed 130 people at the time. The toll is now given as 132, because victims' associations count two survivors who later died by suicide. CNN counted 494 wounded; the Irish Times wrote of more than 500. In the years that followed, the Bataclan was reopened, one conspirator was captured after four months on the run, and in 2022 a Paris court convicted all 20 defendants in the longest trial in French judicial history, according to the Irish Times.

CNN's timeline starts at about 9:20 p.m., when an explosion went off outside the Stade de France in Saint-Denis. President Francois Hollande was in the stadium and was evacuated safely. A second blast followed at 9:30 on the same avenue, and a third at 9:53 on a nearby street. The BBC, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported that a first bomber had reportedly been stopped at a security check and detonated his belt after backing away, and that the attackers all wore identical explosive vests. Four people died at the stadium, according to CNN: three bombers and a pedestrian. AP described Manuel Dias as the first person killed that night, in the first blast; his daughter Sophie spoke in 2025 at the stadium gate where he died.

While the stadium emergency was still unfolding, gunmen in a black Seat pulled up at the junction of Rue Alibert and Rue Bichat in the 10th arrondissement at about 9:25 p.m. The BBC's account quotes a witness at Le Carillon bar who first took the noise for a firecracker. Fifteen people died at the bar and the neighbouring restaurant Le Petit Cambodge, and the BBC reported more than 100 bullets fired. At 9:32 five more people were killed outside Cafe Bonne Biere on Rue de la Fontaine au Roi. At 9:36 the attackers reached La Belle Equipe on Rue de Charonne and fired on the terrace; 19 people died there, making it the second deadliest site of the night. A few minutes later a man who prosecutors later said was Brahim Abdeslam blew himself up inside the Comptoir Voltaire restaurant on Boulevard Voltaire, seriously injuring one person. In all, AP gives 39 dead on the café terraces.

The Bataclan was the deadliest site. The Guardian reconstructed the evening from witness accounts. A black Volkswagen Polo with Belgian plates had been parked about 300 metres away for some time, with at least three men inside. One of them sent the text message "We've left, we're starting"; the phone was later found in a bin near the hall with a floor plan of the Bataclan in its memory. The Guardian named two of the occupants as Samy Amimour, 28, a former bus driver from Drancy, and Omar Ismail Mostefai, 29, and said a third gunman had not yet been identified when it wrote. The BBC's list of the three Bataclan attackers includes Foued Mohamed-Aggad, 23.

The BBC puts their entry at 9:47 p.m.; CNN's timeline says 9:40. The men shot at people smoking outside and then went into the hall and opened fire on the crowd of about 1,500. The Guardian reported that the band stopped playing and ran off, and that many in the audience first thought the noise was part of the show. "It looked like a battlefield," one concertgoer, Marc Coupris, told the paper. "There was blood everywhere, there were bodies everywhere."

At around 10 p.m. a police officer and his driver fired on a gunman on the stage and his explosive jacket detonated, the BBC reported. The two remaining attackers retreated to a corridor on the upper level and took hostages. One of them, a man identified only as Stephane, told the BBC that 11 or 12 hostages were held for two and a half hours, and that the gunmen told them they belonged to the Islamic State and were there to avenge wives and children in Syria. The hostage takers asked hostages for mobile numbers to pass to the police, and said they would blow everything up if the perimeter was not pulled back. Shortly after midnight, at about 12:20 a.m., police special forces stormed the corridor. Stephane said that not a single hostage was injured, though a stun grenade went off beside his feet. The two attackers died when their suicide belts exploded, the BBC reported.

The toll in the hall is given as 89 in the 2015 reporting of the BBC and the Guardian, and as 90 in AP's 2025 coverage. A BBC caption to the interview notes that none of the dead in the hall were hostages.

Within days investigators had named most of the assailants. The BBC described a Belgium-based cell that was in close touch with Islamic State in Syria, and the Guardian said the same. The suspected organiser was Abdelhamid Abaaoud, a 28-year-old Belgian from Molenbeek in Brussels. The French interior minister, Bernard Cazeneuve, said that Abaaoud had played a "decisive role" and was suspected of involvement in four of the six plots French intelligence had foiled that year. The Guardian also reported that he was the subject of European and international arrest warrants, that he had travelled into and through the European Union from Syria at least twice in a year, and that a tip from a non-European agency placing him in Greece reached France only on 16 November, three days after the attacks.

Salah Abdeslam, then 26, was born in Brussels and was a childhood friend of Abaaoud, according to AP. His brother Brahim was one of the dead. The BBC reported that investigators thought Salah had driven the three Stade de France bombers and may have been given a target in the 18th arrondissement, an attack that never happened. He abandoned his vest, called a friend and was driven back to Belgium. The BBC reported that hours after the attacks he and two other men were stopped at least once by police near the Belgian border and allowed to drive on.

Many of the men had been known to the authorities. In the foreword to the parliamentary inquiry report, the commission's president, Georges Fenech, wrote (in French) that all three Bataclan attackers were perfectly well known to the intelligence services and the courts. Amimour had been questioned by the domestic intelligence service in October 2012 and put under judicial supervision, yet travelled to Syria in September 2013 with Mostefai, who was on a security watch list. Mohamed-Aggad was known to French justice for joining Islamic State with nine other men from Strasbourg in December 2013. Fenech also wrote that Salah Abdeslam, listed as radicalised in Belgium, was checked by gendarmes at 9:10 a.m. on 14 November on his way back north; because Belgian services had not entered the radicalisation information in the shared European database, they had to let him go.

French police raided an apartment building in Saint-Denis on 18 November. According to CNN, a suicide device was detonated and shots were exchanged for almost an hour, one floor collapsed and three people died. The Guardian reported that the siege lasted seven hours and that eight people were arrested. Prosecutors confirmed the next day that Abaaoud's body had been found in the rubble, identified from skin samples. A woman police identified as his cousin, Hasna Aitboulahcen, also died, though AP called her his niece; the BBC said about 5,000 bullets were fired during the raid.

The hunt for Salah Abdeslam lasted four months. Belgian prosecutors said his fingerprints were found at an apartment in Forest, Brussels, which police raided on 15 March 2016. A man believed to be an accomplice, Mohamed Belkaid, was shot dead by a police sniper after officers were fired on, and two others escaped. Three days later, on 18 March, Abdeslam was shot in the leg and detained in Molenbeek, the neighbourhood where he grew up, according to AP. Belgium sentenced him in April 2018 to 20 years over the shootout with police, and he was extradited to France in April 2016 on charges relating to the Paris attacks.

CNN reported that in November 2016 French officials identified the suspected coordinator as Oussama Atar, believed to have directed both the Paris attacks and the Brussels bombings of 22 March 2016, which killed 32 people.
content.h2: Emergency rule and the parliamentary inquiry
content.p: Hollande declared a state of emergency on the night of the attacks and closed the borders, and on 16 November asked parliament to extend it by three months. It lasted until 1 November 2017, when a new anti-terrorism law took its place. The Christian Science Monitor reported that the law gave police wider powers to search property, conduct electronic eavesdropping and close places suspected of preaching hatred. Human Rights Watch complained that France had become "addicted" to the state of emergency, and a poll in early October 2017 found more than 80 percent public support for the bill.

A parliamentary commission of inquiry, chaired by Fenech with Sebastien Pietrasanta as rapporteur, filed its report on 5 July 2016. Fenech's foreword described the intelligence services as too complex and badly coordinated, and said information sharing needed to improve. As quoted by the World Socialist Web Site, Pietrasanta said that Amimour's supervision should have been much stricter and that Abaaoud should have been arrested in Greece in January 2015. The Greek authorities had located him in Athens but could not detain him because the Belgian services had not warned them early enough, Fenech wrote. The World Socialist Web Site, which criticised the report from the left, counted 40 proposals, among them recruiting at least 2,000 more security staff and integrating the competing intelligence services and internal special-forces units.

The trial opened on 8 September 2021 in a courtroom built inside the Palais de Justice on the Île de la Cité for about 7 million euros, according to the BBC. The Justice Ministry told the BBC that nearly six years of investigation across 19 countries had produced 47,000 depositions. Twenty men were judged, of whom 14 were present; the other six, tried in absentia, were believed to be dead, apart from one held in Turkey, the BBC said. Abdeslam was the only defendant accused of taking part in the attacks themselves, according to CNN.

Early in the trial Abdeslam described himself as an "Islamic State soldier." By the end he apologised to victims and said he had decided at the last moment not to detonate his vest: "I am not a murderer. I am not a killer." The presiding judge, Jean-Louis Peries, said on 29 June 2022 that the court found the vest had malfunctioned, which "seriously puts into doubt" his account. He was found guilty on all five counts and sentenced to life without parole, which CNN said made him the fifth person in France to receive that sentence since it was introduced in 1994.

Anadolu Agency listed the other sentences. Mohamed Abrini, the "man in the hat" filmed with the Brussels bombers, received life with a minimum term of 22 years; Mohamed Bakkali, Osama Krayem and Sofien Ayari received 30 years each. Others received terms from two to 18 years, except Ahmed Dahmani, held in Turkey, who received 30; five men believed dead, including Oussama Atar, were sentenced to life in absentia. Farid Kharkhach, who forged documents for the group, was the only defendant not convicted of terrorism offences and was sentenced to two years.

On 12 July 2022 Abdeslam's lawyers, Olivia Ronen and Martin Vettes, said he had given up his right to appeal. They added that this did not mean he accepted the verdict, only that he had "resigned himself to it." Nobody else appealed either, Paris Attorney General Remy Heitz said, so the verdicts became final.

The Bataclan itself reopened on 12 November 2016 with a performance by Sting, CNN recorded. The main association of survivors and families, Life for Paris, announced in June 2022 that it would wind down and close on the tenth anniversary. Its president, Arthur Denouveaux, who escaped the Bataclan, told NPR the group had always intended to disband then. NPR also described a 12-year study led by the historian Denis Peschanski that follows nearly 1,000 people, and which found that people's memories of the cafes and the stadium are foggier than those of the Bataclan.

On 13 November 2025 President Emmanuel Macron and Paris mayor Anne Hidalgo visited each site in turn, and AP reported that Hollande and former prime minister Manuel Valls joined families at the Bataclan. The names of the 39 people killed on the café terraces were read aloud. In the evening Macron inaugurated the November 13 Memory Garden opposite City Hall, a stone enclosure from which granite blocks engraved with the victims' names rise to evoke the attack sites. "The pain remains," Macron wrote.
